newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada court to hear homosexual fired from college.
newsitem.headline: Canada court to hear homosexual fired from college.

text.p: The Supreme Court agreed on Thursday to hear an appeal by a homosexual who was fired by a Christian college, in a potentially far-reaching dispute on how far Canadian courts can force an end to discrimination.
The appellant, Delwin Vriend, was dismissed in 1991 as a laboratory coordinator at The King's University College in Edmonton, Alberta, which has strong religious views against homosexuality.
Vriend asked an Alberta court to declare that Alberta's human rights act violated the federal constitution's Charter of Rights since it does not ban discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.
The court agreed and ordered the provincial legislature to include protection for homosexuals in the human rights act.
But the Alberta Court of Appeals overturned that decision in February in a stinging rebuke of what it termed "judicial legislation."

Justice John McClung said in his majority opinion that the Alberta legislature had repeatedly declined to add sexual orientation to the human rights act and said homosexuals and heterosexuals were equally protected in areas the law covered.

In dissent, Justice Constance Hunt said the "legislative silence" on sexual orientation violated the federal Charter of Rights, which provides for "equal protection and equal benefit of the law without discrimination."
Vriend appealed, and his case would have died if the Supreme Court had not agreed to hear it.
